## Why this note exists

The $(\Delta,R)$ counterfactual test-inversion (see `9999-elvis.qmd`'s Counterfactual section) came back with a real problem: the auxiliary revenue moment's own standard error was enormous ($\approx559$ COP), making every confidence set uselessly wide — adjacent $\Delta$'s were statistically indistinguishable from each other. This note explains the fix that was adopted: a **control-variate correction** to the auxiliary moment, a classical Monte Carlo/simulation variance-reduction technique (@Hendry1984, §on efficiency-improving simulation designs; the same device is called CUPED in the modern causal-inference literature and the "regression estimator" in survey sampling). The point of this note is to make the case, precisely, that this is a pure efficiency gain — same estimand, smaller variance — not a re-specification of what the auxiliary moment identifies.

## Where the noise was coming from

The auxiliary moment tests candidate mean revenue $R$ via
$$g_{R,i}(\Delta) = \frac{R_i(\Delta)}{pgdp_i} - R, \qquad E[g_{R,i}]=0 \iff E[R_i(\Delta)]=R.$$

Diagnosed directly (a new `dvecdiag` C++ mode dumping the full moment vector and its sampling SEs at a fixed $(\theta,\gamma)$, no optimization): `se`$(g_{R,i})\approx559$ **at every tested cell**, unaffected by MCMC chain length (`n_keep` 300 to 30,000, SE unchanged to 4 significant figures) — confirming this is a **between-firm** quantity, sample variance of $R_i$ across the $n=32{,}232$ firms, not a simulation-noise artifact. It's driven by raw firm-size heterogeneity: the firm's own observed $t1_i$ (sales tax paid on sales — fully exogenous, no model dependence) predicts the model-implied $R_i(\Delta)$ almost perfectly, $R^2\approx0.999$ pooled across the whole tested $\Delta$ range, slope $\hat\beta\approx0.999$. That makes economic sense: $R_i=t1_i-\tilde\tau_P[M_i+(1-q)e_i']$, and the evasion-credit term is a comparatively small, weakly-size-correlated correction on top of $t1_i$'s own scale.

## The correction

Since $c_i\equiv t1_i/pgdp_i$ is fully observed (no latent variable, no estimation uncertainty) and highly correlated with the target, replace the moment with
$$g_{R,i}^{\text{adj}}(\Delta) = \Big[\frac{R_i(\Delta)}{pgdp_i}-\hat\beta\, c_i\Big] - \big[R-\hat\beta\,\mu_c\big],\qquad \hat\beta=0.998838,\ \ \mu_c=E[c_i]=2507.602596$$

both **fixed, precomputed constants** — $\hat\beta$ from a preliminary OLS fit of a forward-simulated $R_i(\Delta)$ on $c_i$ (pooled across all tested $\Delta$'s for robustness, not re-derived from a single $\Delta$), $\mu_c$ the plain sample mean of a fully-observed covariate. Neither is a new ELVIS decision variable — the dimension of $(\theta,\gamma)$ is unchanged.

**The target is provably untouched.** For *any* constant $\hat\beta$, $E[\hat\beta c_i]=\hat\beta\mu_c$ cancels on both sides, so $E[g_{R,i}^{\text{adj}}]=E[g_{R,i}]$ exactly. Verified numerically too: the adjusted and raw sample means agree to 6+ significant figures at every tested cell. **Only the variance changes** — by construction, $\text{Var}(g_{R,i}^{\text{adj}}) = \text{Var}(R_i) - 2\hat\beta\,\text{Cov}(R_i,c_i)+\hat\beta^2\text{Var}(c_i)$, minimized at the OLS $\hat\beta$. Empirically: `se`$(g_R^{\text{adj}})\approx14$–$15$ at every tested cell, a $38$–$41\times$ reduction, with the resulting hard-test confidence sets now closed and non-overlapping across adjacent $\Delta$'s on the tax-increase side — the actual problem this was built to solve.

## Why not just add industry$\times$year fixed effects?

TWFE is the same idea with a saturated-categorical control instead of a continuous one — subtracting each firm's own industry$\times$year cell mean is algebraically identical to regressing on a full set of dummies. Checked directly rather than assumed: additive industry+year FE barely helps (SE $559\to508$); the full interaction (318 cells) gets real traction (SE $\to223$, $R^2=0.84$) but needs 318 new nuisance parameters and has genuine small-cell risk (100 of 318 cells have $<30$ observations). The continuous control variate does far better ($38$–$41\times$) with zero added dimensionality, because firm size — which $t1_i$ tracks almost exactly — is the dominant driver of revenue dispersion, far more than which industry-year cell a firm happens to sit in; once $t1_i$ is controlled for, industry$\times$year adds almost nothing further ($R^2$ $0.9993\to0.9994$).

## Conceptual FAQ: what exactly is being reduced?

"Variance reduction" invites a sloppy reading — that the CI just got narrower by fiat. It's worth being precise about which of several distinct notions of "error" is actually being touched here, since the terms get used loosely even in the source literature.

**Disentangling the vocabulary.** *Bias/accuracy* asks whether $E[\hat\mu]=\mu$ — the center of the sampling distribution. *Variance/efficiency/precision* asks how spread out that distribution is around its center, at fixed $n$ — three words for the same axis. The *sampling distribution of the estimator* is the distribution of $\hat\mu=\frac1n\sum_i g_i$ across hypothetical re-draws of the $n\approx32{,}232$ firms from the underlying population — the object whose variance sets the CI width. *Simulation (Monte Carlo) error* is a different, additional layer: the per-firm moment $g_i$ isn't observed exactly, only approximated by an MCMC average over draws of the latent $M_i$, which injects its own noise on top of the cross-sectional sampling variance. And the *distribution of the unobservables* — $f_\psi$, or more precisely the entropy-tilted conditional law of $M$ given $Z$ that $\gamma$ selects — is a separate object entirely, untouched by any of this. The `dvecdiag` diagnostic (SE unchanged from `n_keep=300` to `30,000`) already settles which of these the original $\approx559$ SE came from: not simulation error. It's ordinary finite-$n$ sampling variance of $\bar g_R$ across the actual firms in the data — dominant, and, as far as this correction is concerned, essentially the whole story (simulation error is confirmed negligible, not merely assumed away).

**Translating Hendry/Davidson's index.** @Hendry1984 (§4.3) and @Davidson1992 build control variates over Monte Carlo *replications* $j=1,\dots,N$ — redraws of an entire synthetic dataset, a meta-experiment device for characterizing an estimator's own sampling distribution more precisely without running more replications. Davidson & MacKinnon's regression $t=\theta\iota+\lambda\tau+u$, with $\hat\lambda$ the OLS coefficient on the control and $V(\hat\theta)/V(\bar t)\to1-R^2$ asymptotically, is exactly the identity behind $\hat\beta$ and the $38$–$41\times$ reduction above — but their index $j$ is a *replication*, and this note's index $i$ is a *firm*. There is no meta-experiment here — no redrawing of the whole dataset many times — just the identical regression-based device applied one level down, directly to the cross-sectional sample average already sitting inside the GMM/CUE moment. Mechanically indistinguishable from Hendry/Davidson's construction; conceptually closer to the regression/ratio estimator in survey sampling (Cochran) or to CUPED in causal inference, where the "replications" being averaged over are cross-sectional units, not simulation draws.

**What's actually being isolated.** Since $c_i\equiv t1_i/pgdp_i$ is fully observed with $E[c_i-\mu_c]=0$ by construction, subtracting $\hat\beta(c_i-\mu_c)$ is Hendry's (27)–(28) exactly: unbiased for *any* $\hat\beta$, variance-minimized at the OLS value. What gets removed is the part of $\text{Var}(R_i(\Delta))$ that's linearly predictable from firm scale — and that part carries no information about $\Delta$ specifically *because* $\tau_S$ (hence $t1_i$) never moves in this exercise, not because size-heterogeneity is generically uninformative. That's the actual license, and it's the same reason a control variate built from something that *could* plausibly respond to evasion (industry, $K$, $L$) would be a materially shakier choice than $t1_i$ — see the TWFE comparison above. What's left untouched throughout: the estimand $E[R_i(\Delta)]$ (every firm still contributes weight $1/n$, no reweighting, no conditioning, no subsample restriction), the tilted distribution of the unobservables (governed separately by $\gamma$), and the simulation-error layer (a distinct, empirically negligible, source of noise this correction was never aimed at).

**Why this isn't a numerology trick.** Two conditions carry all the weight: $\hat\beta,\mu_c$ must be fixed constants, not re-estimated jointly with $(\theta,\gamma)$ at each grid cell (else the correction could adapt to the hypothesis under test); and $c_i$ must be exogenous to $\Delta$ (true here, since only $\tau_P$ is shocked). Under those two conditions, a mis-specified $\hat\beta$ costs efficiency, never validity — bias is exactly zero for any $\hat\beta$, which is the entire point of the device. Both conditions hold here by construction (§"The correction" above), so the tightened CI reflects real information already in the data ($t1_i$, fully observed, known to be $\Delta$-irrelevant), not an artifact of how the correction was built.

**The residual variance is not just noise.** After the correction, what remains splits into two pieces: genuine identifying signal — firm-level variation in evasion response that depends on $(\theta,\gamma)$, which is exactly what gives the test power to separate candidate $R$'s — and irreducible idiosyncratic noise. This is why the correction stops at one clean continuous control rather than chasing further variance reduction with covariates that could themselves be correlated with evasion behavior: doing so would risk laundering signal out along with noise, trading a validity problem for an efficiency gain. It is also what the 2026-09-14 free-$\theta$ robustness check (see `9999-elvis.qmd`'s Counterfactual section) was built to confirm directly — that the CV moment's sharpness traces to real cross-firm heterogeneity in evasion response, not to an artifact of holding $\theta$ fixed at each cell.

## Bottom line

This is an efficiency improvement in the ordinary econometric sense of the word: the same population object — $E[R_i(\Delta)]$, exactly what the auxiliary ELVIS moment was already built to recover — estimated with a lower-variance moment. No new identifying assumption, no change to $(\theta,\gamma)$'s dimension, no distortion of the other nine moments' own fit (checked: $\text{dvec}[0..8]$ is identical whether the raw or adjusted row 9 is used, at a fixed $\gamma$). It's the same logic as adding a covariate in a randomized-experiment estimator (ANCOVA/CUPED) or a poststratified survey mean — the target doesn't move, only how much of the outcome's variance gets treated as irreducible noise before the test statistic is formed.
